directions: Plant bare-root seedlings in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Antonovka is grown chiefly as an extremely cold-hardy rootstock or grafting understock rather than for its own fruit. A historic Russian apple selection prized above nearly all other apple rootstocks for exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating winter temperatures that kill or severely damage most other apple rootstocks, making it the standard understock for grafting desired apple varieties in the coldest northern growing regions of North America. Trees grown from Antonovka seed produce full-sized, vigorous trees rather than the dwarfing habit of modern clonal rootstocks, and the fruit itself, while edible, is tart and primarily used for cooking and processing rather than fresh eating. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young Antonovka seedlings in late winter or early spring for a cold-hardy, long-lived, full-sized tree well suited to harsh northern climates.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Geneva 41 is grown as a dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Geneva 41 is grown as a dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit. Developed by the Cornell University and USDA apple rootstock breeding program at Geneva, New York, this modern dwarfing rootstock produces a small, highly productive tree roughly 40-50 percent the size of a full-sized seedling tree, with outstanding resistance to fire blight and Phytophthora root rot, two of the most serious diseases limiting older rootstocks like M9 and M26. Its combination of size control, disease resistance, and precocious early fruiting has made it one of the most widely adopted modern dwarfing apple rootstocks in commercial and high-density home orchards. Provide permanent staking or trellising, since the small, brittle root system does not anchor well without support, and graft a desired named variety onto young rootstock in late winter for best results.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Bud 9 is grown as a fully dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; Bud 9 is grown as a fully dwarfing understock, not for its own fruit. Bred in Russia and among the most cold-hardy of the fully dwarfing apple rootstocks available, it produces a small, highly precocious tree roughly a quarter to a third the size of a full seedling tree, bearing fruit remarkably early, often within two to three years of grafting. Its combination of extreme size control and superior winter hardiness compared to similarly dwarfing rootstocks like M9 has made it a favorite for high-density home and commercial orchards in cold-winter regions. Provide permanent staking or trellising, since its small root system anchors poorly without support, and expect a compact, easy-to-harvest and easy-to-spray tree well suited to a small home orchard.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M111 is grown as a semi-dwarfing to semi-standard understock, not for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired apple variety onto the young rootstock; M111 is grown as a semi-dwarfing to semi-standard understock, not for its own fruit. One of the classic Malling-Merton series rootstocks developed in England, it produces a vigorous, semi-standard-sized tree that develops a large, sturdy, self-supporting root system needing no permanent staking, along with good drought tolerance and adaptability to a wide range of soil types compared to the smaller, more demanding fully dwarfing rootstocks. Its self-supporting, low-maintenance root system and tolerance of poor or dry soil have made it a traditional standard for larger home orchard trees and for growers unwilling or unable to install permanent trellising for dwarf trees. Graft a desired named apple variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and give the eventual tree ample room, since it grows nearly as large as a full seedling tree.

planting.note: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock.

directions: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock. A long-standing standard peach seedling rootstock widely used across commercial and home orchards for its reliable vigor, good compatibility with a broad range of peach and nectarine varieties, and adaptability to a range of well-drained soil types. It produces a full-sized, vigorous tree without the size control offered by modern clonal dwarfing rootstocks, making it best suited to a home orchard with ample space for a standard-sized peach tree. Graft a desired named peach or nectarine variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide well-drained soil, since peach rootstocks in general are notably intolerant of wet, poorly drained conditions.

planting.note: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock; Nemaguard is bred specifically for root-knot nematode resistance.

directions: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach or nectarine variety onto the young rootstock; Nemaguard is bred specifically for root-knot nematode resistance. Bred specifically for strong resistance to root-knot nematodes, a serious soil-borne pest that stunts and kills peach trees on susceptible rootstocks in warm, sandy-soil growing regions, it has become the standard rootstock for peach and nectarine production across the sandy soils of the Southeast, Gulf South, and California. Its nematode resistance makes it a far more reliable choice than ordinary seedling rootstocks for a home orchard on sandy or previously peach-planted soil, where nematode populations often build up over time. Graft a desired named peach or nectarine variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and note that it is somewhat less cold-hardy than other peach rootstocks, best suited to zone 7 and warmer.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach, plum, or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; Citation is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach, plum, or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; Citation is a dwarfing understock, not grown for its own fruit. A California-bred interspecific hybrid rootstock valued for producing a semi-dwarf tree roughly two-thirds the size of a standard seedling tree across a wide range of stone fruit species, including peaches, nectarines, plums, and apricots, offering rare cross-species versatility compared to most rootstocks bred for a single fruit type. Its size control makes for an easier-to-manage, easier-to-spray, and easier-to-harvest home orchard tree than a full-sized seedling rootstock, while still tolerating heavier soils better than some other dwarfing stone fruit rootstocks. Graft a desired named stone fruit variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide moderate staking support while the semi-dwarf root system establishes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Toringo crabapple is a wild species used both as an ornamental tree and, historically, as breeding stock for many modern crabapple cultivars.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Toringo crabapple is a wild species used both as an ornamental tree and, historically, as breeding stock for many modern crabapple cultivars. Small, pink-budded flowers opening white cover this graceful, small Japanese species tree in spring, followed by tiny, pea-sized, red-to-yellow crabapples that persist into fall and provide food for birds, and the wild species has served as important parentage in breeding many modern disease-resistant flowering crabapple cultivars grown today. Its small mature size, graceful branching habit, and reliable disease resistance compared to many older crabapple cultivars make it a worthwhile small ornamental tree in its own right, not merely a footnote in crabapple breeding history. Water during establishment, then rely mainly on natural rainfall, and prune minimally to maintain its naturally graceful form.
